vnotes: Source ambiguous: Sapir treats stress and pitch-accent as one prominence: the accented syllable obligatorily carries one of 'two or three musical inflections' with contour minimal pairs (se'el 'black paint' vs sel 'kingfisher', p.20) = tonal under the catalog's definition (pitch-accent system, no placement rule stated: 'It is impossible to give any simple rule for the determination of the proper accent of all words', p.20); …
1716.dq: Nevertheless a fully accented word is normally stressed on some particular syllable; it may even happen that two forms differ merely in the place of accent
1716.dloc: sec. 5 'Stress and Pitch-Accent', pp. 15-16 and p. 20; also sec. 26 p. ~55 and Conclusion p. 283
1716.prule: No positional stress rule. A fully accented word is stressed on some particular (lexically/grammatically determined) syllable, and the stressed syllable obligatorily bears one of 'two or three musical inflections' (raised, rising, falling); raised and rising are length-conditioned counterparts (raised only on final short vowels or shortened diphthongs, rising only on long vowels and diphthongs: 'The rising pitch is for a long vowel or diphthong what the raised pitch is for a short vowel or shortened diphthong'), so on a given accented syllable the contrast is falling vs. non-falling. Words and grammatical forms may differ solely in place of accent (naga'-ida£ 'when he said' vs naga-ida'£ 'when you said') or solely in pitch contour (se'el 'black paint' vs sel 'kingfisher'). Sapir: 'It is impossible to give any simple rule for the determination of the proper accent of all words'; accent placement is 'of a grammatic, not purely phonetic, character'. One sub-generalization: a glottal catch requires falling pitch on the immediately preceding stressed syllable, with 'but few exceptions' (a small class of transitive verbs with long vowel and rising pitch before the catch in the 1sg-subject/3-object aorist, e.g. k!eme£n 'I make it'). In connected speech unemphatic words are often accentless (proclitic/enclitic); sentence-finally a syllable that normally has falling pitch 'may sometimes, though by no means always, assume a raised accent'.
1716.quote: As in many Indian languages, the stress-accent of any particular word in Takelma is not so inseparably associated with any particular syllable but that the same word, especially if consisting of more than two syllables, may appear with the main stress-accent now on one, now on the other syllable. In the uninterrupted flow of the sentence it becomes often difficult to decide which syllable of a word should be assigned the stress-accent. ... Nevertheless a fully accented word is normally stressed on some particular syllable; it may even happen that two forms differ merely in the place of accent…
1716.loc: sec. 5 'Stress and Pitch-Accent', pp. 15-16 and p. 20; also sec. 26 p. ~55 and Conclusion p. 283
1716.idn: Takelma (river/Lower Takelma of the middle Rogue River; the upland dialect is excluded); data: Siletz reservation, Oregon; a month and a half in the summer (July-August) of 1906; single informant Mrs. Frances Johnson, born c. 1845 at Dak'ts!asin village on Jump-off-Joe Creek (Rogue River), mother from upper Cow Creek
1716.exq_: It is impossible to give any simple rule for the determination of the proper accent of all words.
1716.tone: Sapir describes 'a system of syllabic pitch-accent' (p.9) giving the language 'a decidedly musical character'; the stressed syllable takes one of three musical inflections (raised, rising, falling), notated after the Lithuanian pitch-accent convention; minimal pairs differ only in pitch-accent (se'el/sel, he'el 'song'/hel 'sing it!'); 'Pitch-accent is of grammatical importance, but is most probably a product of purely phonetic causes' (sec. 26); Conclusion: 'a system of pitch-accent of fairly considerable, though probably etymologically secondary, formal significance'. Stress and pitch accent coincide on one syllable; its position is not phonologically predictable.

1718.prule: Weight-conditioned, hedged (Arden para. 29): in a word with both long and short vowels 'a certain amount of emphasis naturally falls upon the long' -- his example குமாரன் kumāraṉ 'son' has the long vowel, and hence the emphasis, in the SECOND syllable; when all vowels are short, or all long, 'the emphasis is always thrown upon the first syllable' (maram, aṉuppu, avar; never the second as in English support/refresh). Default = initial. The modern instrumental source (Keane 2004/2006) states no weight condition and no fixed position: no lexical stress, 'the location, and even existence, of stress are disputed', initial syllables have 'some phonetic prominence' inferred from non-initial vowel reduction, and F0 differences are only 'consistent with' abstract initial word-level prominence cued by phrasal pitch accents, with no consistent duration or loudness correlate.

1720.prule: Two-tone system (A high / B low, syllable = TBU, lexical tonal melodies AA/BA/AB, BAA/AAB contrastive); stress is predictable and non-contrastive, falling on the first high-toned syllable of the word (one accent per word, including compounds). Position therefore varies with the lexical tone melody (initial in ˈAAB, second in BˈAA, final in BBˈA), not with syllable count or weight.
1720.srule: Secondary accent (hedged, 'puede haber' / 'al parecer'): where a word has a second high-tone span after the one bearing the primary accent, a secondary accent may fall on that next high tone — in the verbal word on the present suffix -ɟu when it surfaces H (ex.28a,c,e,f), and in compounds with two high tones on the next H of the second member (ex.26d-e, 113a). Tone-conditioned, not rhythmic; not marked in the transcriptions (fn.144).

tn.quote: La lengua se caracteriza por el empleo de la altura tonal, como rasgo distintivo. Hay dos tonos puntuales, A (alto) y B (bajo). Los tonos se asocian a la sílaba, cuyo ámbito de realización es la vocal, la cual le sirve de unidad portadora de tono (UBT). ... La minimalidad silábica está relacionada con la combinación de los patrones tonales AA, BA, y AB, melodías tonales que en bases verbales bisilábicas oponen sentido ... El acento en tanimuka es un acento predecible, que recae en la primera sílaba de tono alto. Strom (1992) habla de un acento distintivo, sin hacer alusión a los tonos.
tn.translation: The language is characterised by the use of pitch height as a distinctive feature. There are two level tones, A (high) and B (low). The tones associate to the syllable, whose domain of realisation is the vowel, which serves as the tone-bearing unit (TBU). ... Syllabic minimality is related to the combination of the tonal patterns AA, BA and AB, tonal melodies that distinguish meaning in disyllabic verb bases ... Accent in Tanimuka is a predictable accent, which falls on the first high-toned syllable. Strom (1992) speaks of a distinctive accent, without alluding to tones.
tn.cite: Eraso, Natalia. 2015. Gramática tanimuka, una lengua de la Amazonía colombiana. PhD thesis, Université Lumière Lyon 2 (HAL tel-01582502).
tn.note: Two level tones (H/L), lexical melodies on bases (AA, BA, AB; 3-syll. BBA AAB AAA BAA ABA; no *BB/*BBB); accent predictable on the first H. Tone phonetics and a word-final mid tone left unstudied. morph.rootq: Ochiai 2016 §2.2 p.14: 「多音節語の強勢は、例外なく次末音節に落ちる。」 ('In polysyllabic words stress falls without exception on the penultimate syllable.') ... 「接語は強勢を担わない。」 ('Clitics do not bear stress.'); §6.6.1 p.114: 「これら[-i, -e/-o, -un, -an]が接尾辞として付くと、もともと次末音節にあった強勢の位置が後ろへ 1 音節ずれることになる。」 ('When these are attached as suffixes, the stress that was on the penult shifts one syllable rightward'); §6.6.2 p.115: with the disyllabic suffixes -ani/-ane/-anun stress 'shifts two syllables back and falls on the first syllable of the suffix (-áni, -áne, -ánun)'. I.e. the domain is the suffixed word (root+suffixes), excluding enclitics; the rule is not stated on the root.
morph.elicq: Ochiai 2016 §2.2 p.14: 「強勢の位置は、単独で発音した場合に顕著である。しかし、文中に埋め込まれた場合、全ての多音節語が強勢を持って発音されるわけではない。文は述部と主部に分かれるが、この 2 区分における機能語や接語を除く最終語の次末音節に強勢が置かれ、その他の音節は平板に発音される。」 ('The position of stress is conspicuous when [a word is] pronounced in isolation. However, when embedded in a sentence, not every polysyllabic word is pronounced with stress: ... stress is placed on the penult of the last word, excluding function words and clitics, of each of the two divisions [predicate / subject part]'), followed by sentence examples (1)-(9) with stress marked; fieldwork elicitation with three speakers (§1.4 p.11); no instrumental measurements (fn.4: 'this point needs further investigation').
morph.stmt: Ochiai 2016 §3.1 p.35: 「接辞には、接頭辞、接中辞、接周辞、接尾辞がある。これら接辞が付くことで、動詞の他動性を決定するほか、時制(現在・過去・未来) や法(命令・勧誘) が表される。」 ('Affixes comprise prefixes, infixes, circumfixes and suffixes; their attachment determines the verb's transitivity and expresses tense (present/past/future) and mood (imperative/hortative)') — i.e. a mixed profile: actor voice, future, stative, causative, reciprocal, non-volitional and denominal marking are prefixal/infixal (<um>, <un>, mu-, pu-, muCu-, tu-, su-), undergoer/locative/circumstantial voice, imperative/hortative and most nominalisers are suffixal (-un, -an, -i, -e/-o, -ani, -anun), and person (NOM/GEN pronouns) and possessors are second-position enclitics.

1730.heavy: Only explicit weight definition in reached text is Pulipaty 2019's own constraint set (adopting Kolachina 2016): 'I propose here the following metrical OT constraints for Telugu.... WSP: Heavy syllables are stressed. WEIGHT-BY-POSITION: Coda consonants are moraic.'; poster grid (3c) marks dam.mi.ɖi: heavy-light-heavy (CVC and CVV both macron) and (1b) dammiɖi: 'CV́ C.CV̀.CVV'. The older descriptive rule (Sitapati 1936, Sailaja 1985) is carried only as 'light'/'heavy', undefined in the carrier; Lisker & Krishnamurti 1991 (carried) phrase the perceptual tendency in terms of long vs short vowels only.
1730.dflt: initial (descriptive tradition); the L&K 1991 perceptual study instead reports a weak second-syllable tendency
1730.prule: Non-contrastive word stress; descriptive tradition (Sitapati 1936, Sailaja 1985, Kelley 1959/63, Kolachina 2016): primary stress on the first syllable, but on the second syllable when the first is light and the second heavy (left-edge two-syllable weight window, default initial).
1730.srule: Secondary stress on every alternate mora after the primary-stressed mora, except the word-final mora, with no two adjacent stressed moras; in a heavy (CVV/CVC) syllable the stress falls on its first mora -- equivalently left-to-right bimoraic trochees (Kolachina 2016, carried by Pulipaty 2019). Pulipaty 2019 revises the details: every head of a moraic-trochee foot is stressed (all heavy syllables, plus light syllables heading an (LL) foot in a left-aligned parse), the leftmost head primary and the others secondary, so stress is not strictly alternating, final heavy syllables take secondary stress and clash is allowed, e.g. (é.ni)(mì.di), (vá:)(hì.ni), (pá.ri)ki(ɳì:), dé:vìɖì:. Secondary stresses are inferred from resistance to vowel harmony (and syllable duration, Kolachina p. 36), not from speaker intuition.

morph.rootq: §2.1.2.2 p.44: 'In Quechuan languages stress typically occurs on the penultimate syllable, and TK is no exception in this regard. ... In certain cases, however, stress falls on the ultimate syllable. This tends to be the case for disyllabic ideophones, e.g. tulún tulún ... It also applies to nouns affixed with the locative marker -y ... /'pun.dza/ 'day' vs /pun'dza-i̯/ day-LOC ... They also list other suffixes which shift the word stress of their hosts to the last syllable: the present tense suffixes /-n/ (3SG) and /-nun/ (3PL), as well as the suffix /-nɡax/ [PURP] ... in my corpus the interaction of the suffix /-n/ with stress seems to be optional.' Also §3.4.2 pp.228-229: enclitics =ri…

The stressed syllables were identified based on the qualitative analysis of the correlates (pitch, intensity, duration).' §3.4.2 p.229: 'The above analysis of the marker's interaction with lexical stress relied, as mentioned previously, on auditory and pitch contour analyses.' evidence_works.detail: Lección 7 '(Acento: Grave)' states that in Runa shimi almost all words are stressed on the syllable before the last: 'Runa shimíi ñalla tucui shimiunara Puchucai Ñaupajpi Uyarijta mas shinzhi rimanchi, casna: qui-hua, in-di, ta-ru-ga, ri-cun-chi-mi, ma-qui-sa-pa-ra, a-pi-mush-can-gui-chu.'. Lección 8 '(Acento: Esdrújula)' then lists the two exception classes with written accents: final-stressed 'aguda' forms '(Puchucaibi mas shinzhi uyarijca mishu shimíi aguda ninaun). [...] casna: micuushcái, paihuáj, pujlláun, rimangáj, callpanáun, ucúi.' and antepenultimate 'esdrújula' forms, all of whose listed examples end in -ga or -mi: '(Chita mishu shimíi antepenúltima nishcái shinzhi rimajta esdrújula ninaun). [...] casna: yáyaga, mámaga, állcuga, rimáshaga, ríjpiga, cújpiga, chimándami, raushcaráicumi.'. The work states no rule for the enclitics themselves; its grave (penultimate) examples in Lección 7 include 'ri-cun-chi-mi', so it does not establish -mi as a non-shifting enclitic. The glossary repeats the three-way scheme: 'Puchucai uyarij mas shinzhi uyarin - Acento aguda'. Nothing on secondary stress.

1733.prule: Stress is usually on the penultimate syllable (Carter 1952: 231). In words whose final vowel has been dropped the stress may remain on the now-final (originally penultimate) syllable or shift back to the new penult (revasini > revasin, 'stress on either of the last two syllables'); one pair is distinguished by stress alone (pote 'shame', first syllable, vs pote 'like, as', last syllable).

1736.prule: Non-contrastive word stress: primary stress on the last heavy (long-vowel) syllable of the lexical morpheme; if the morpheme has no heavy syllable, on its penultimate syllable; monosyllabic phonological words stress their only syllable; otherwise certain inherently stressed suffixes take stress. tn.quote: KT is a tone language in which every syllable carries one of three underlying tones. In isolation, the three tones are realized as high to low falling (HL), low to high rising (LH), and a low (L) tone which is fairly level but downglides before pause. ... In terms of realization, where a higher number represents a higher pitch, HL = 41, LH = 23, and L = 21. ... Although a word carries only HL, LH or L in isolation, tones are modified in context, where a fourth tone, high (H), is observed, as well as contrastive downstep (↓).

tn.note: Three tones on every syllable (isolation HL, LH, L), analysed as /HL, H, L/ from two levels; contours = H+L sequences; contrastive downstep, floating tones, spreading. No stress statement in Hyman.

tn.quote: There are three tone levels, H[igh], M[id], and L[ow]. None of these can be reduced to an allophone of one of the others. There is no evidence in favor of an accentual interpretation of tones. Contour tones on individual syllables, other than those due to vv-Contraction across boundaries. are <HL> and <LH>. <MH> is predictably disallowed since M would drop to L before H by the tone sandhi rule M#H-to-L#H (§3.6.2.2). ... These comments apply mainly to non-verb stem-classes since verbs (other than compounds and Jula borrowings) have level-toned stems.
tn.cite: Heath, Jeffrey & Aminata Ouattara. 2021. A Grammar of Tiefo-D of Daramandugu (Niger-Congo language, Burkina Faso). Language Description Heritage Library; Zenodo record 4715103, doi:10.5281/zenodo.4715103.
tn.note: Three level tones H, M, L; syllable contours HL and LH treated as tone sequences; verbs level-toned, nouns carry melodies (LH, rarer HL); M drops to L before H; elided article leaves a tonal trace. corr.words: the article undergoes vv-Contraction and is effectively absorbed into the preceding vowel. It often leaves a tonal trace, in case its tone prior to its deletion was different from the tone of the preceding syllable. ... That is, the tone of the contracted vowel moves toward the M-tone of the deleted ē. ... The à or á disappears segmentally, but leaves a tonal trace.

tn.quote: Tigemaxo has three lexical and grammatical tone levels, H (x́), M (x̄), and L (x̀). … In Tigemaxo, bimoraic Cvv and Cvⁿ syllables may be level-toned or bitonal. Level-toned syllables may be H, L, or M. Bitonal bimoraic syllables are falling <HL>, <HM>, and <ML>, and rising <LH> but not stepwise rising #<LM> or #<MH>. Only <HL> is stable in all positions in the clause. … The tone-bearing unit is the mora, as shown especially by the frequent occurrence of Cv́v̀ and Cv́v̄ syllables. Monomoraic Cv generally allows only one tone.
tn.cite: Heath, Jeffrey. 2025. A Grammar of Tigemaxo of Dia (Bozo family, Mali). Language Description Heritage Library. Zenodo, record 15160216.
tn.note: Three tone levels H, M, L on the mora; stems carry lexical melodies (/H/, /M/, /HM/, /HL/, /HLH/, rare /LH/, /LHL/) with grammatical overlays and terracing; phonetic downstep; no word-level accent.

Raz: stress is non-distinctive and shifts easily between syllables; prominence is organized by a stress-timed rhythm into 'stress units' (bounded by sharp transitions, each containing at least one prominent stress) that cut across word and affix boundaries; in his interrogative examples the primary stress falls on the last syllable of the stress unit.
1742.srule: Not mentioned in Raz 1983, sec. 2.2.1-2.2.4 pp. 7-8 (the word is not a stress domain; Raz only says a stress unit contains 'at least one prominent stress' and, in interrogatives, distinguishes a prominent stress on the particle mi from the primary stress on the unit's last syllable -- phrasal, not word-level). Also not mentioned in Elias 2014, sec. 2.16 pp. 28-29.
1742.quote: [Raz 1983 p.7] The accentual system of Tigre cannot be described in terms of word boundaries, as is the case in many languages. This is, firstly, because stress is non-distinctive and shifts easily from one syllable to the other. Secondly, a certain speech rhythm is maintained by means of which the number of prominent stresses in a given utterance determines the length of time it takes to produce the utterance.
